One Hundred Years of Solitude: Memory, Destiny and the Fall of Macondo

Mostafa Auvi (মোস্তফা অভি) · 2026-10-31

Standing before the firing squad, Colonel Aureliano Buendía did not think of a battle, or of any revolution. He thought of an afternoon when his father took him to a gypsy tent to see ice. Ice is only frozen water, cold and quick to melt. Yet José Arcadio led his son to it by the hand as though the world were opening a door. That man would later go mad and be tied to a tree in the yard, rain running down his body. His wonder, though, did not die with his sanity. It lived on in the son, who had started thirty-two uprisings and lost every one. At the end, all that came to him was a small boy staring.

Úrsula Iguarán had married her cousin, and her mother had warned her that such marriages produce children with pigs’ tails. It sounds funny now. Úrsula did not find it funny. She went to bed each night in a kind of chastity garment, laced tight so her husband could not reach her. Could a strip of cloth hold back fate? She knew it could not. She wore it anyway. Clever people do foolish things when they are afraid. The family later fled the village after a killing and founded Macondo beyond the mountains, but the fear came along in the luggage. Years afterward, a child was born with a tail. Úrsula understood then that you can change the place without changing the wound.

Macondo grew by small steps: a few houses, then a street, then shops. Melquíades and his gypsies arrived with magnets and telescopes, and José Arcadio lost his head over the magnets. He was sure they would pull gold out of the earth. He chased the idea day after day, forgot to sleep, forgot his family, and left Úrsula to carry the household alone. What is a magnet? A piece of iron that attracts other iron. He made of it the key to a gold mine. I have seen men like him in my village, men who catch a small chance and believe everything will change. They buy land, build a second storey, open a stall at the market. A few succeed. Nobody keeps track of the rest. Even his madness had a logic. The earth, he said, is round like an orange. He was right, and nobody much cared.

The names in the Buendía family keep returning: José Arcadio, Aureliano, Úrsula, Amaranta. At first you lose track of who is whose father. Then a pattern emerges. The José Arcadios are bulky and impulsive, the Aurelianos quiet and withdrawn. But the appetites are not the same from one to the next. The first chased magnets, another chased power, another only the strength of his own body. Same blood, same restlessness, with only the object changing. My grandfather’s name went to a nephew of mine, and everyone said the boy had his temper. Nobody asked why the temper came down and the kindness did not. The Buendías, too, seem unable to walk their own road. They step into the footprints of the dead.

Úrsula lived nearly a hundred years at the center of the house. She saw births and weddings, the mischief of great-grandchildren, the rise of the family and its fall. She made candy animals and sold them, saved her money, added rooms. While her husband chased his experiments, while Aureliano was at war, while Amaranta sank into herself, Úrsula was in the kitchen. Nobody looked at her, yet the house stood on her shoulders. I have known grandmothers like that. Up before dawn to sweep the yard, then prayers, then cooking, and at night, after everyone else has gone to bed, the last one to bolt the door. Her name is half forgotten, but if she died the house would fold in a day. Úrsula’s real grief was that she saw everything and could stop nothing. In old age she understood her children. The Aurelianos had clear minds but kept their distance, and the José Arcadios were warm but weak. That was her defeat: knowing them, and not being able to save them.

As a boy, Colonel Aureliano sat alone in his father’s workshop making little gold ornaments, hour after hour, without a word. Then one day he left for the war. Thirty-two uprisings, thirty-two defeats. Seventeen sons, all seventeen murdered. He tried to kill himself and lived. In the end he came back to the same workshop and began again to make little gold fishes, melting them down and remaking them. A man crosses a whole country in arms and ends up exactly where he began. His life was a circle with no outside. I keep thinking about the old soldier’s remark that the dead are easier company, since they ask for nothing. I wonder whether there was anger in his eyes when he said it, or only weariness, and the thought makes me shiver. Nothing is lonelier than a hero saying that.

Remedios the Beauty is the strangest figure in the book. She is so lovely that men die looking at her. One falls from a roof, another trails her until he vanishes into the desert. Remedios herself understands none of it. She won’t wear clothes, won’t help with the house, and bewilders everyone. One afternoon, folding sheets in the yard, she rises into the sky with them and never comes back. García Márquez writes it in the flat voice of someone reporting weather, and the onlookers just stand there with their mouths open. But under that lightness there is an ache. No one on this earth could hold her, or love her properly. Every village has people like this, the ones we call odd. We avoid them, or we laugh. It may be that they are the ordinary ones, and we are not.

Fernanda del Carpio came to Macondo expecting to be a queen. Her family had once been grand, and only the pride had survived. She married Aureliano Segundo and never accepted the town as hers. Church, prayer, heavy curtains, everyone kept at a distance. Her husband loved parties and kept a mistress, and their marriage was a daily war. Her worst damage, though, was to her own daughter. Meme fell in love with Mauricio Babilonia. Fernanda would not allow it. Mauricio was shot and left crippled, and Meme was sent to a convent. Fernanda believed she was saving her. In truth she lived inside a tomb of her own, and she dragged her daughter down into it. There are mothers like this everywhere, burying their children in the name of honor. Fernanda wasn’t wicked. She never learned that there was a door.

Then the banana company came. A railway was laid, electricity arrived, foreigners moved in, and the town changed almost overnight. But the prosperity was not Macondo’s. The company ran everything. When the workers went on strike, three thousand of them gathered in front of the station. Soldiers opened fire. The bodies were loaded onto a train. The next morning the town woke to find everything in order, as if nothing had happened. Those who spoke of the dead were called mad. Something like this really did occur in Ciénaga, Colombia, in 1928, and García Márquez wrote it into the novel. What stays with me is how he shows an event being erased. People forget because it is almost impossible to live otherwise. We, too, know of days and bodies for which there is no account anywhere.

Near the end the rain begins and lasts four years, eleven months and two days. Houses give way, streets go under, people leave one by one. Úrsula dies, then Fernanda, then Aureliano Segundo. The house empties. Only Aureliano Babilonia remains. He shuts himself in Melquíades’s room to decipher the parchments and realizes that the whole history of the family was written there beforehand, down to the very moment of his reading. Before he can finish the last lines, a great wind rises, and Macondo is wiped from the earth.

I put the book down for a long while after finishing it. It felt as though the entire novel had been sealed inside a manuscript. Melquíades wrote, Aureliano read, and when the reading ended, everything ended. Melquíades himself was an outsider, a gypsy who arrived with magnets and telescopes, but his real gift was those pages. For years no one could read them. Then someone did, and after that nothing was left. Is that what García Márquez is saying, that a family or a town exists only as long as someone reads it? And if no one reads? I don’t know.

The novel is not flawless. In places the middle seems rushed. Arcadio’s rule is over almost before it begins. The last generation, Aureliano Babilonia above all, never takes on the blood and weight of the early characters. Perhaps the speed is the point, a way to show the slide toward ruin, but as a reader I wanted him to slow down and stay a little longer with them. Then again, life is untidy too. Some people we remember sharply, some barely, and not everyone’s story gets told equally.

Reading Gregory Rabassa’s English is the usual way in for most of the world, and in Bengali I read G. H. Habib’s translation, and both left me thinking how hard it is to hold on to García Márquez’s voice. His sentences pile up, one on another, and move like a river. Habib tries to catch that current and often does. The line about the world being so recent that many things lacked names, and you had to point a finger to speak of them, stands in his Bengali exactly as it does in the original. Elsewhere the Bengali takes a few words too many and the prose loses its breath. Still, the book reads well, and you feel that Macondo lives on in Bengali as well.

When you finish One Hundred Years of Solitude, it feels like a big house has been emptied. The doors are open and dust covers the yard. Children once played here, Úrsula cooked, José Arcadio sat in his workshop. Now there is only dust. And yet somewhere in the dust you can hear laughter, crying, footsteps. My grandmother used to say that when a person dies, their smell lingers a few days and then fades. The smell of Macondo has not faded. It rises from the pages, cold like ice, damp like rain. Perhaps that is what Melquíades wrote down, so that someone might one day read it and learn that a town can outlast its ruin, living only in the writing.
